part_title: Training Data, Labels and Structured versus Unstructured Information
review_basis: Original AIF Module 03 slides 15–18 visually inspected: poor data in/out, dog/cat labeled examples, structured customer/time-series tables and unstructured review/audio/visual examples.

scenes.title: Training Data
scenes.narration: Before any machine-learning model can make useful predictions, it needs examples to learn from. That is what training data means. Start with the left panel showing crumpled papers. The message is sometimes called garbage in, garbage out: if your examples contain mistakes, unfair gaps or incorrect values, a model can learn misleading patterns. Imagine training a program to recognize cats and dogs, but most dog pictures have the wrong label. The program might learn a pattern that does not match real animals. A high-quality dataset should represent the actual situations the application will face, and it should be checked for duplicates, missing values, errors and bias. Bias means systematic differences that make the model less reliable or unfair for certain groups or cases. Move to the middle panel. A labeled example has a known answer attached, such as the photograph of a dog with the label dog. Unlabeled data has an image or document but no target answer. Both can be useful, though they support different learning approaches. On the right, data can be structured as rows and columns, like a customer table, or unstructured, like pictures, audio and ordinary text documents. The bottom example shows pictures going into an animal recognition model and a new photograph receiving a prediction. Notice the distinction: training uses the existing examples to develop the model, while inference uses the finished model on a new image. If the training examples all came from bright studio photographs, the system may struggle with a blurry nighttime photo. That is why data quality and coverage matter. Check your understanding: would adding ten thousand incorrect labels necessarily improve a model? No. More examples do not repair incorrect or unrepresentative data. Start by choosing the right examples and verifying that their answers are trustworthy.

scenes.title: Labeled vs. Unlabeled Data
scenes.narration: Let's compare two datasets containing the exact same animal photographs. On the left, each image has a label underneath: cat, dog, cat and dog. The label is the answer attached to that example, not merely a filename or a decorative description. A supervised learning algorithm can use these pairs to learn how visual patterns relate to the correct category. Later, when it sees a new photo, it predicts the category. On the right, the animal photographs are present but the answer cards contain question marks. That is unlabeled data. An unsupervised learning method might discover that some photographs look similar and form groups, but it has not been given the human answer dog or cat for each one. The diagram underneath turns that distinction into a simple formula: input plus known label supports supervised learning; input without target labels can support unsupervised methods such as clustering. Clustering means grouping examples according to learned similarities. Now look at the bottom customer-support example. A ticket saying cannot log in to account has an urgency label High. A password-reset question is Medium, while a feature request is Low. Those labels could be used to train a priority classifier, but only if the organization has defined and checked the categories consistently. On the right the same messages have no urgency labels. We could explore groups of related messages, but we cannot assume the groups automatically match the organization's priority levels. For a short test, imagine a university has five hundred past student questions already categorized into admissions, fees and exam dates. What learning style is naturally suited to predicting a category for a new question? Supervised classification because the previous examples have known labels. If the messages have no labels and the university only wants to discover common topics, clustering may be a useful starting point.

scenes.title: Structured Data
scenes.narration: Structured data is information organized into a predictable format. Look at the table on the left. Each row represents one customer record, while columns contain the customer ID, name, age and purchase amount. The customer ID identifies the record, while age and purchase amount are example features, meaning attributes that can be used in analysis. We must not assume every available column is an appropriate feature: identifiers, personal information and data collected after the outcome can cause privacy or modeling problems. Next, follow the middle time-series table. Here each row is a date and a stock price. Time-series data means measurements collected in chronological order, so the sequence and timing matter. The picture shows January first through fifth and example prices ranging around two hundred dollars. Those values are illustrative, not market forecasts. The arrow moves the organized data toward an analysis or machine-learning system, and the final panel shows charts and insights. A business could use structured purchase records to calculate monthly sales or predict demand. The computer can operate on rows and columns more consistently because the meanings of fields are defined. Yet structured does not mean correct: missing ages, duplicate customers, inconsistent currency symbols and inaccurate dates still require cleaning. For machine learning, we often separate the known target from the input features. For example, if the goal is to predict whether a customer will cancel, the actual cancellation outcome may serve as a training label when it is available. Practice question: is a spreadsheet showing date, temperature and rainfall structured data? Yes, if each row follows a consistent table schema. Is a scanned handwritten note automatically a structured table? No, it may need document recognition and extraction first.

scenes.title: Unstructured Data
scenes.narration: The three images across the middle represent data that does not fit neatly into a fixed table of fields. On the left, documents, articles, chat messages and reviews contain natural language. Two reviews may discuss the same product using completely different words and lengths. In the center, photographs, scanned forms and diagrams store visual information as pixels rather than ordinary database columns. On the right, audio recordings and videos contain signals unfolding over time. These forms are called unstructured data because their raw content lacks a uniform predefined row-and-column schema. This does not mean they are meaningless or impossible to organize. A photograph can have structured metadata such as its date and filename, while its pixel content is still unstructured. Now read the customer-review examples on the right. One customer says the product works well. Another praises shipping. A third says the product is good but the packaging arrived damaged. We cannot capture all those details just by storing a star rating. An AI application could analyze sentiment, identify topics such as delivery or quality, or extract specific complaints. Sentiment analysis tries to determine attitudes expressed in text, but it can make mistakes with sarcasm and context. Likewise, speech recognition may convert audio to text before another system analyzes it. The key takeaway at the bottom is that unstructured data can carry rich information, but it often needs processing to make that information searchable or usable by machine-learning models. In the decision cue, ask whether the information is already a consistent table. If not, consider techniques appropriate to documents, images, audio or video. Quick example: a table of product IDs and prices is structured data. A folder of customer-submitted product photographs is unstructured image content. And a database may contain both types together. Always choose processing based on the actual input and the question you need to answer.
